newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: LatAm markets' correlation to Dow grows - study.
newsitem.headline: LatAm markets' correlation to Dow grows - study.

text.p: The correlation of Latin American financial instruments with the Dow Jones Industrial Average has risen shaprly in the last three years, says a study by Argentina's Economy Ministry.

The shift towards the Dow has replaced the importance of the U.S. 30-year Treasury bond as the main influence on the price movement of many Latin American instruments, said the internal study, of which Reuters obtained a copy Wednesday.
For instance, in 1994 Argentina's par Brady bond had a 91.9 percent correlation with the 30-year long bond and only 12.4 percent with the Dow.
By the beginning of this year, the correlation with the Dow was 69.6 percent against 9.4 percent with the bond.

The report found that the correlations of Mexican and Argentine financial instruments had showed the greatest shifts towards the Dow away from the benchmark U.S. Treasury, while Brazilian paper showed just higher correlation with the Dow.

In 1994, Mexico's par bond had 84.6 percent correlation with the bond and 16.4 percent correlation with the Dow compared to just 3.5 percent with the bond and 75.9 percent with the Dow at the beginning of this year.
The report said one of the reasons Brazil's market correlations were different was the Real Plan, introduced in July 1994, which boosted Brazil's markets.

In 1994, Brazil's par bond had a 39.1 percent correlation with the Dow and 5.5 percent with the 30-year bond, while at the beginning of this year the correlation with the Dow was 75.1 percent and 1.5 percent with the bond.

Brazil's Bovespa stock index showed a similar development with its correlation with the Dow at 44 percent and 5.3 percent with the bond in 1994, compared with 79.5 percent with the Dow this year and 6.6 percent for the 30-year bond.

Still, this year "the possibility of decoupling from falling U.S. markets will obviously depend on the size of the hike in U.S. rates because of its impact on Latin American debt servicing charges," the report stated.

The perception of and the maintenance of the region's economic rebound and the development of politics, considering there are elections in Argentina and Mexico this year, will be especially important in deciding on the correlation of Latin America's markets with the U.S. in 1997, added the report.
